Image symmetry

Source: R/symmetry.R
img_symmetry.Rd

img_symmetry returns the vertical and horizontal mirror symmetry of an image. Higher values indicate higher image symmetry.

Usage

img_symmetry(img, vertical = TRUE, horizontal = TRUE, exact = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

img

An image in form of a matrix or array of numeric values. Use e.g. img_read() to read an image file into R.

vertical

logical. Should the vertical symmetry be computed? (default: TRUE)

horizontal

logical. Should the horizontal symmetry be computed? (default: TRUE)

exact

logical. Should the correlation be computed directly for every position of the mirror axis instead of locating the best position with a fast Fourier transform? This is considerably slower and only rarely leads to a (minimally) different result (see details). (default: FALSE)

...

Further options: shift_range to shift the mirror axis, per_channel to switch between a maximal per channel vs. per image symmetry (see details).

Value

a named vector of numeric values (vertical and horizontal symmetry)

Details

The function returns the vertical and horizontal mirror symmetry of an image img. Symmetry values can range between 0 (not symmetrical) and 1 (fully symmetrical). If vertical or horizontal is set to FALSE then vertical or horizontal symmetry is not computed, respectively.

As the perceptual mirror axis is not necessarily exactly in the middle of a picture, the function estimates in a first step several symmetry values with different positions for the mirror axis. To this end, up to 5% (default) of the image width is cut off on the left or on the right side of the image (in the case of vertical symmetry; analogously for horizontal symmetry), and the symmetry of the remaining image part is computed. As the mirror axis is always in the middle of the remaining image part, cutting off 5% of the image width shifts the mirror axis by up to 2.5% of the image width to the right or to the left. In the second step, the overall symmetry score is computed as the maximum of the symmetry scores given the different mirror axes. See Mayer & Landwehr (2018) for details.

Advanced users can change the shift range with the optional parameter shift_range, which takes a numeric decimal between 0 and 1 as input (the maximum share of the image width that is cut off). The default is shift_range = 0.05 (i.e., 5%).

Symmetry cannot be computed if one of the image halves has no variation (e.g., an image half that has only one color; for color images, this applies to each color channel). In this case, the function returns NA for the respective symmetry and throws a warning. For color images with a color channel that has no variation (e.g., an image that only consists of black and red), consider converting the image into grayscale first (see rgb2gray).

For color images, the default is that first a maximal symmetry score (as explained above) is obtained per color channel (parameter per_channel = TRUE). Subsequently, a weighted average between each color channel's maximal score is computed as the image's overall symmetry. Advanced users can reverse this order by setting per_channel = FALSE. This results in first computing the weighted averages for each position of the mirror axis separately, and afterwards finding the maximal overall symmetry score.

To keep the computation fast, the best position of the mirror axis is located with a fast Fourier transform (FFT), which yields the symmetry values of all positions of the mirror axis at once. The symmetry score for this best position is then computed directly as the correlation between the two image halves. The result is the same as when the correlation is computed directly for every position of the mirror axis, unless the symmetry values of two positions are practically tied (difference smaller than about 1e-10). In this rare case, the score might differ by a correspondingly small amount. Setting exact = TRUE computes the correlation directly for every position of the mirror axis (the method used up to version 1.0.1), which avoids this at the expense of speed (the computation takes several times longer; for large images, more than ten times longer).

A perfectly symmetric image (i.e., the two image halves are identical mirror images of each other) always receives a score of exactly 1.

References

Mayer, S. & Landwehr, J. R. (2018). Quantifying Visual Aesthetics Based on Processing Fluency Theory: Four Algorithmic Measures for Antecedents of Aesthetic Preferences. Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 12(4), 399–431. doi:10.1037/aca0000187

See also

img_read, img_complexity, img_contrast, img_self_similarity, img_simplicity, img_typicality

Examples

# Example image with high vertical symmetry: rails
rails <- img_read(system.file("example_images", "rails.jpg", package = "imagefluency"))
#
# display image
grid::grid.raster(rails)
#
# get symmetry
img_symmetry(rails)
#>   vertical horizontal 
#>  0.9551137  0.1230616 

# Example image with low vertical symmetry: bridge
bridge <- img_read(system.file("example_images", "bridge.jpg", package = "imagefluency"))
#
# display image
grid::grid.raster(bridge)

#
# get symmetry
img_symmetry(bridge)
#>   vertical horizontal 
#>  0.4803173  0.2526229 

# compute the correlation directly for every position of the mirror axis
# (slower)
img_symmetry(bridge, exact = TRUE)
#>   vertical horizontal 
#>  0.4803173  0.2526229
